articles.text: In an update on pickleball use at the Linda-Beach courts, Recreation Department Director Chelle Putzer announced at a Recreation Commission meeting on April 19 that the department created a QR code with four questions when players check in: how many people are in your group playing, what type of transportation did you use, how long are you going to play, and the number of residents in your group. From March 1 to April 19, Putzer said, the courts had 2,883 check-ins, 60% of which were Piedmont residents. Slightly more than half of the users planned to play for one to two hours. Commissioner Amir Virani noted that the QR survey did not distinguish between participants who dropped in for organized drop-in play and informal drop-in play. He recommended that in the future the QR survey provide such a distinction for arriving players. The Beach courts are open for pickleball play from 9 a.m. to dusk, Monday through Friday. Putzer confirmed that the Recreation Department has “received consistent noise complaint[s] since the start of the [five-month] trial.” To address the complaints, the department will work to find “an acoustical consulting firm to perform some noise measurements.” Pickleball players were encouraged to use noise-dampening paddles provided by the department. Defending the noise complaints, Amy Vallerie said she is “still…disappointed about this Commission’s decision to go forward with this trial, despite having a petition of 250 neighbors about how this trial was arranged, conducted and communicated. For the past six weeks the tone, volume, and popping of pickleball paddles has permeated our homes despite doors and windows mostly being closed.” She recommended that the commission schedule pickleball on courts throughout the city “so that it does not negatively impact one neighborhood.” Another neighbor, Pierre Garrigues, said, “I’ll take kids playing any day before pickleball paddle noise, and I think it changes the feel of the neighborhood when we hear the constant pickleball paddles.” He agreed with Vallerie’s suggestion of “spreading the usage of pickleball across the town.” The Recreation Commission will invite community feedback on pickleball play at the Beach courts again at its meeting on Wednesday, June 21. Community members can send questions and comments about the pickleball trial to BeachPickleballTrial@ piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: Piedmont’s community reading project, Readmont, now in its 13th year, has selected No Stopping Us Now by Lucy Jane Bledsoe as this year’s collective read. Led by Piedmont High School English Department Chair Beth Black, Readmont will host a community discussion with the author tonight, Wednesday, April 26 at 7:00 p.m. in the Ambassador Chris Stevens Library. The book was chosen to help celebrate the 50th anniversary of Title IX, the federal legislation requiring equal funding for women’s and men’s sports. It is a book about the love of sports, finding one’s own voice, and activism. Based on the author’s true story, the book follows the story of Louisa who fought to bring her hometown into compliance with the new Title IX law so she could play basketball at her high school in Oregon. Those interested in discussing the book and learning more about the author are encouraged to attend the evening event. English department chairperson Black will also lead discussions during lunchtime on April 25 and 26. For more information, contact Kathryn Levenson, Teacher Librarian at Piedmont High School at klevenson@piedmont.k12.ca.us (510-594-2781), or Beth Black, PHS English Department chairperson, at bblack@piedmont.k12.ca.us. No Stopping Us Now by Lucy Jane Bledsoe was named a Finalist for both the Golden Poppy Award and the Rainbow Award. For 24 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmont-post.com, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken.

articles.text: Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC), a coed Venturing unit with Piedmont Scouts, has served local youth ages 14-20 for two decades, providing much more than an easy way to find service opportunities. As a part of Piedmont Council BSA it follows principles of youth empowerment and actively encourages teens to take on responsibility and give them creative license with guidance so that they gain practical life skills. It hosts service trips, including a plan to build tiny houses in Medford, Oregon this June. The Crew’s largest annual project, renovating a low-income Oakland resident’s house in conjunction with the non-profit Rebuilding Together Oakland (RTO) is now underway. This year’s ambitious project involves rebuilding an entry deck needed for access to the home; replacement of a large window that has been broken for many years; renovation of a bedroom and bathroom damaged by rats and water leaks; and repair of a leaking tub drain. Crew members and parents work together with parents on the RTO project, enjoying teamwork, learning new practical skills, and meeting the homeowners who are grateful and constantly in awe of the work done by the teen members of the Piedmont Community Service Crew. The home restoration project is funded entirely by the crew. Maddy Tran and Stephanie Lee learn drywall patching skills. Mark Modera (left), a long-standing adult contributor and advisor with the RTO projects, discusses plans with Tolganai and Simon March Cunningham during the early phase of the deck rebuilding project. Amelia Carter, all suited up, helps clean up a very dirty bedroom and bathroom. Invitation to new members Teens and adults are encouraged to join now and take part in this once-a-year event. Work days have been scheduled every Saturday and Sunday through mid-May. Middle school families PCSC has a middle school companion club, Piedmont Service Club. Middle schoolers register annually and come to events with their parents. Most of the activities for PCSC youth (age 14 or 8th grade graduates) are open to middle school members, but not the RTO project. Community adults are also encouraged to become involved in PCSC. The crew is youth led, but the teens benefit from adults who mentor them. Some adults engage by being regular crew volunteers at a particular activity of their choosing. For example, cooking meals for the food insecure at College Ave. Presbyterian Church allows crew members to plan a menu, shop for the food, and lead their peers in cooking. Adult volunteers help the youth leaders to plan in advance and help solve problems when they occur. Register your teen now for the Community Service Crew and get the rest of this crew year for free (new memberships submitted between now and May 10 will be good through May 10 next year. articles.text: Piedmont Education Foundation is pleased to welcome 11 individuals to the Board of Directors for the 2023-24 fiscal year. After a thorough process of nominations and interviews, the board voted to approve Jade Cameron, Marco Gonzalez-Navarro, Michael Gross, Kim Hunter, Judy Lin, Dana Murray, Ashish Patel, Max Roman, Julia Ruthven, and Jennie Stomberg. Sara Davison DeVries has returned to the board after a two-year hiatus to lead the middle and high school parents clubs and Sara Davison DeVries returns to help lead the grantmaking process “We are thrilled to introduce our incoming slate of board members — a group of accomplished individuals who bring a wealth of expertise and a shared passion for our mission,” said Board Chair Amelie Kappes. Jade Cameron, an expert in employment law, joins PEF because of shared values of community, engagement, and connection. Professor Marco Gonzalez-Navarro wants to help Piedmont schools continue to thrive. Michael Gross is an active member of Beach Dad’s Club, and Kim Hunter, while working as an assistant district attorney, has volunteered toward the success of the Giving Campaign, Harvest Festival, Spring Fling, and other PEF fundraisers. Judy Lin currently leads operations for the largest non-profit educational partner of the National Parks Service and looks forward to building resources for PUSD. Dana Murray and Julia Ruthven co-chaired this year’s successful Giving Campaign and both bring exceptional marketing, analytical and communications skills to the board. Dr. Ashish Patel has significant executive-level board experience and will bring that expertise to PEF, and Max Roman, a Piedmont native, wants to use his skill with investments and negotiations to ensure his children have an even better educational experience than he did. Jennie Stomberg, a forensic accountant, brings important audit and governance skills to PEF. “As we welcome new board members, we also bid farewell to some of our long-standing members whose unwavering commitment and valuable contributions have helped shape our organization,” said Kappes. Leaving the board are Cortney Allen, Francis Hoang, John Orta, Sarah Puckett, Rick Smith, Linda Smith Munyan, and Rebecca Thornborrow. “That was the year Dude stopped to smell the roses.”

articles.text: As the Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization (PRFO) enters the final stage of fundraising for the new Piedmont pool facility, it thanks the community for coming together to raise the funds necessary to complete the project. Every dollar raised will go directly to completing the pool complex, ensuring that it meets the needs of the community for decades to come. “The dream of creating a world-class aquatic facility is nearing a reality,” said PRFO President Steve Collins. “Over 250 community members have committed from $50 to $500,000 to help reshape central Piedmont. Significant progress has been made towards fully matching the $500,000 anonymous gift announced in January, and there is still time to double your impact. There is also one naming opportunity remaining within the pool facility. Those interested should contact Eric Havian PRFO Fundraising Chair. The campaign, which began in September 2022, will end on June 1, 2023. Contributions of any amount are welcome and all gifts $500 or more made prior to June 1 will receive prominent recognition at the new facility. To keep residents informed about the progress of the project, the City has installed a camera for construction updates that can be viewed at https://piedmont. ca.gov/government/projects/piedmont_community_pool. articles.text: Last week 619 teams and over 35,000 people from 18 countries attended the 4-day FIRST Robotics Competition World Championship in Houston. Piedmont’s Team 8033, the Highlander Robotics, finished 3rd in their division, placing them in the top 1.5 percent of all competitors internationally with their robot. Paddo the Frog. The FIRST Robotics Competition, which frames high school robotics as a full contact sport complete with mascots and cheering sections, announces a new game in January of each year to be played by two alliances of three robots in an arena about the size of a basketball court. An entirely new robot must be constructed for each season and competitions start in the sixth week. In this year’s game, Charged Up, robots up to 125 pounds and 6-feet-6-inches tall score points by collecting and placing 9.5- inch inflatable cubes and 1-foot high rubber cones in a grid of poles and pedestals as well as by balancing robots on a see-sawlike platform called a “charging station.” Teams who qualified for the World Championship at regional tournaments in seven countries were placed into eight divisions. Each team plays 10 qualifying rounds with randomly selected partners, after which the highest ranked eight teams become alliance captains and draft three others to work with throughout Mechanical Lead and pit crew member Chloe Kessinger does last minute checks before Paddo’s next match. the double-elimination playoff brackets. Draft selections are key to success in the playoffs and all teams at the elite level dedicate time to track every robot’s performance across 125 qualifying rounds in a process called “scouting.” The Highlanders ended the first day of qualifications on Thursday ranked 36th of 77 in their division. On Friday they continued to perform well with 3 wins and 2 losses and moved up to 19th place while maintaining a rank of 3rd in overall scoring. The Highlanders were picked in the first round of the draft by the 8th seed alliance captained by the Mountie Megabots from Jackson, Michigan and joined by two Israeli teams. In the first round of the double elimination playoffs, the Highlanders lost 208-189 to the 1st seeded alliance, citrus Circuits from Davis. After a first-round loss the Highlanders won three straight matches in the lower bracket to reach the semifinals where they faced faced Citrus Circuits, seeded 1st. Citrus Circuits led for the entirety of the match but in the last 25 seconds the Highlanders whittled a 25--point lead down to 4, 185 to 181 in favor of Citrus Circuits. Citrus Circuits and their alliance went on to win the Galileo division and were eliminated in the final field by an alliance from Madera. A team from Guelph, Canada went on to win the Championship. Paddo the Frog was operated by Vaughn Khouri and Matteo Scanu, supported by drive coach Alex Ware, technician Nate Hart, and human player Paddo, the Highlanders’ robot, features a 3-stage elevator with a wheel-based intake on a wrist that is used for picking up and placing cones and cubes. Ava Grochowski. Helena Young and Peter Stokes led the pit crew which kept the robot running smoothly through 15 full contact matches. Jasper Tripp led scouting and strategy operations with 13 scouts and a software team led by Cassie Colby, Jessica Liu, Caetano de Figueiredo, and Tiago de Figueiredo acted as ambassadors who fielded questions and built connections. Highlander Robotics was founded in 2019 by brothers Henry and Charlie Lambert and now has 54 members from Piedmont High, Millennium, College Prep, Las Lomas, Stanford Online High, Lick Wilmerding, Maybeck, Monte Vista, Head Royce, and Bentley. They work out of the Mary G. Ross Engineering Lab at Piedmont High School. For more information contact Kevin Clark at kevin.clark@ gmail.com or visit https://frc8033. com/. articles.text: Young People’s Symphony Orchestra has announced that its annual Spring Concert will be performed on Saturday, May 13, at 7:30 p.m. at First Congregational Church of Berkeley, 2345 Channing Way. David Ramadanoff, now in his 34th season with the 101- piece youth orchestra, will conduct a performance of Brahms’ Academic Festival Overture, Symphonic Metamorphosis of Themes of Carl Maria von Weber by Paul Hindemith, and Maurice Ravel’s LaValse. It will also feature two Concerto Competition winners, violinist Noa Marvit performing the First movement of Symphonie Espagnole by Édouard Lalo, and Ethan Chen in von Weber’s Concertino for Clarinet in E-flat. Founded in Berkeley in 1936, YPSO is the oldest youth orchestra in California and the first independent youth orchestra in the nation. Tickets are $20 and are available online at http:// www.ypsomusic.org/tickets and at the door. For more information call (510) 849-9776 or visit http:// www.ypsomusic.org.

articles.text: What does a focus coach do? I hear this question a lot when I tell people what I do for a living and for good reason. Though ADHD is well known, focus coaching for ADHD is still a relatively new concept. I am a former student of Piedmont schools and I recently started an ADHD focus coaching business, MindsGlowing. I decided to leave my career in tech sales and become a focus coach when I came to realize the unique set of challenges that people with ADHD face when tackling the world around them. I understand these challenges and have faced them in my own life. Before I was diagnosed, I struggled with procrastination, lack of organization, and other ADHD symptoms and it wasn’t until I was diagnosed after college that I began to find relief through medicine and developing systems for myself. After I was diagnosed, I decided to complete a program in Positive Psychology to better understand how the mind works and I now use my certification in Applied Positive Psychology to help people with ADHD achieve their goals. One of my clients is a premedical student at Columbia University who has recently been diagnosed with ADHD. We meet a few times a week for targeted focus sessions where we work on goal setting, craft her to-do lists, and tackling her more difficult projects. My coaching takes many different forms depending on the client, day, and a multitude of factors. I customize each session based on my client’s unique goals and challenges because there is no one size fits all way to coach people with ADHD. I want to introduce one concept, intentional relaxation, which I work on with my clients who struggle with procrastination. The idea behind intentional relaxation is: when you’re watching tv or scrolling through Tik Tok when you’re supposed to do something, it doesn’t feel very good. It becomes hard to enjoy the thing you’re doing when you’re worried about the things that need to get done. To try intentional relaxation, you want to set aside time where you are aware that you’re relaxing and can enjoy it more fully. The best time for this would be when you don’t have too much to do, but you can also use it as a break between two tough tasks or in between school and doing homework. Set a timer for 30 minutes and let yourself watch the show or go on Instagram and really enjoy the time. Once it’s over, you’ll have more energy to complete the task at hand. Check back next month for more on ADHD, focus coaching, and positive psychology tips! Erica Monical is the founder and focus coach at MindsGlowing. articles.text: The Piedmont Planning Commission presented its annual Design Awards to the winning homeowners, architects and contractors at a ceremony at Piedmont Community Hall on Wednesday evening, April 19, at Piedmont Community Hall. The awards recognize and honor the finest of residential work completed in the city in the previous 12 months. This year, seven awards were presented: two for Excellence in Accessory Dwelling Unit (ADU) Design; Excellence in Home Renovation and Expansion; Excellence in a Comprehensive Stylistic Update; Excellence in Landscaping and Outdoor Living; Excellence in Deck Design; and Excellence in Window Replacement. Laurie Schweitzer and Jai Balkissoon of Oakland Avenue were presented with an award for Excellence in ADU Design. The architect was Tim Wooster. Contractors were Wesley Bascom of Lookfar Builders, Lulu Sanchez of Richmond Tile Solutions, Scott Capurro of Capurro Plumbing, and Becca Durkee of Morning Glory Gardens. Schweitzer said that the ADU was expanded during the pandemic from a small garage to a one-bedroom unit, “an attractive example of how Piedmont can meet our housing goals.” Thanking the contractors who worked with her, she added “I don’t know if many people can say they still love their contractors after a project, but I still love mine. We’d intended to rent [the ADU] out as needed, and instead it has become a lovely place we often go, and where our kids stay when they visit.” Regina O’Connor and Jesse Hull of Pala Avenue were also presented with an award for Excellence in ADU Design. Their contractor was Bryan Keane of Custom Construction. O’Connor praised her former garage conversion, located at the back of her property, for the “living space it offers in a city that is quite built out. Within six months, a storage shed became a place where our friends and relatives are excited to visit.” Cori and Zach Kau of Pala Avenue were presented with an award for Excellence in Home Renovation and Expansion. Their contractors were the architect Carolyn Van Lang, and Ry Miller of Madrone Builders. Although he accepted the award, Zach Kau said the project’s completion was due entirely to his wife’s supervision. “When we moved to Piedmont,” he added, “We wanted a master bedroom and bathroom of our own. It’s playoff season at Piedmont High, and the boys’ lacrosse team is leading the charge. Piedmont will face rival Bishop O’Dowd in the championship game on Thursday, April 27. The game will be played at O’Dowd, which is hosting both the boys’ and girls’ title games. Earlier last month on March 17, Piedmont won 18-1. For Piedmont coach Al Yu, defeating Bishop O’Dowd is extra sweet. It was also one of Miya Fujimoto’s best games on the mound with 11 strikeouts in a complete game victory over the Pilots. Fujimoto, the team’s former shortstop, has stepped in to fill the pitching void created by the graduation last year of Izzzy Epstein. 9-3 over St. Joseph Piedmont came out hot with five runs in the first inning and added one more in the bottom of the second. St. Joseph broke the shutout in the top of the fourth, but the Highlanders tacked on two more in the bottom half. The Pilots scored twice in the fifth inning, and the Highlanders scored once more in the sixth. In the bottom of the first Fujimoto led off by reaching first on a well-placed bunt. Mia Leggett then smacked a ground ball and reached first base on an error by the second baseman. With two runners on, Bell cracked a home run to center field. Morgan Hunt then drew a four-pitch walk, while Sa’mara Levi and Hailey Ronen also drew walks to load the bases. Caitlin Boothby then hit a high fly ball to right field, but the outfielder botched the catch, allowing Hunt and Levi to score at 5-0. In the second inning, Hunt hit a one-out single, followed by Levi reaching first on an error by the shortstop, sending Hunt to third. Gretchen Gerhardy then hit into a fielder’s choice to score Hunt for an RBI. In the fourth, Leggett led off by getting hit by a pitch and Hunt reached first on a bunt. With one-out, Levi hit into a fielder’s choice to bring in Leggett from third. Gerhardy then hit a double to score Levi, 8-1. PHS scored one more in the bottom of the sixth, starting with a single by Bell, who stole second and advanced to third on a wild throw into the outfield. Hunt then brought in Bell on a groundout to third. articles.text: =Highlanders defeat Berkeley in semifinals at home Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team will return to the Western Alameda County Conference championship game after defeating Berkeley 11-9 in the semifinals at Witter Field on Tuesday, April 25. Piedmont did well to match up to a physical Yellowjackets team, tiring out the visiting side as the game wore on. “Our game plan was when we get the ball, we’re going to run through our plays. We know Berkeley is not a deep team and they got more tired as the game went on,” said PHS coach Carlton Chan. “In the second half the plays started to open up more.” Piedmont lost 13-12 to the Yellowjackets in last year’s league semifinals 13-12. “We decided in the second half to hold the ball and use our time. We know how physical Berkeley plays and you just have to get back up when you get fouled… That was so difficult last year to lose on our home field. It feels so much better this time around to earn our shot in the finals,” added senior Molly Ashton. The goal all along has been to reach the WACC Finals and square off with Bishop O’Dowd for the league crown, That rematch will take place this Friday, April 28 at the Dragons’ home field. Piedmont went into the league tournament as the No. 2 seed, and O’Dowd enters as the No. 1 seed. “We’re just going to press them. We want to come out quickly and with the same intensity like it was halftime. O’Dowd will be tricky, but I think we can come out with some new plays and catch them off guard. It’s a different game every time against O’Dowd,” said Ashton. PHS now holds an 8-5 overall record and is 5-1 in league. They are assured of being in the Division 2 North Coast Section playoffs regardless of Friday’s result. 11-9 win vs. Berkeley Piedmont led 6-5 at halftime, and boosted it to 11-6 with 4:21 left in the game, but Berkeley finished with three unanswered goals to close it out 11-9. Berkeley opened with the game’s first two goals, but Chloe Graham got Piedmont on the board three minutes in, but the Yellowjackets went up 3-1 one minute later. Graham then scored with 17 minutes left in the first half, followed by Ashton with a wraparound goal 30 seconds later to knot it at 3-3. Piedmont then gained the lead with another goal by Ashton with 8:49 left. She scored one more with 6:56 left in the half. Berkeley tied the game with 5:55 left in the half with back-to-back goals, but Friedie Schickedanz fed Ashton for a goal with 7.9 seconds left to make it 6-5. In the second half after a few back-and-forth possessions, Berkeley scored on a shooting space opportunity with17:34 remaining to tie it at 6-6. But Piedmont then marched back to the front with five straight goals by Ashton with 15:02 left, Ruby Guzdar on a wraparound with 10:39 to go, Ashton fed Eleanor Lavin four minutes later, another Staff Photo Hailey Marshburn runs the ball upfield against Berkeley. Staff Photo Molly Ashton scored six goals against Berkeley and four on the win vs. Newark Memorial. wraparound by Ashton, and Guzdar with a low shot with 4:21 left. Berkeley scored with 3:01 left in the game and again with 2:17. Although the Yellowjackets won possession, Piedmont did well to force tough shots and kept BHS off of the board until 33.9 seconds were left to make it 11-9. No one scored from there. Final stats: Ashton scored six goals with one assist, one ground ball, and won one draw. Graham and Guzdar scored twice. Lavin scored once, recovered one loose ball, and won four loose balls. Schickedanz had three assists. Cole Luisa and Peyton Watson had one assist. Senior Night Piedmont hosted Senior Night on Wednesday, April 19 in a game with Newark Memorial, which resulted in a 19-2 win. PHS honored its five seniors: Ashton, Lavin. Lindsay Kottle, Sofia Johnson, and Holland Feinberg. Final stats: Ashton scored four goals, one assist, recovered two loose balls, and won one draw. Graham and Guzdar had two goals and one assist. Laurel Bentley also scored twice. Schickedanz had two goals and two assists. Johnson had a goal and two assists. Hailey Marshburn, Luisa, and Lavin scored once. articles.text: Jasper Schuetz wins Freshman Div. 1 race Photo by Jane Lin Jasper Schuetz (middle) won his fourth Freshman D1 race of the spring mountain bike season. The Piedmont Mountain Bike team recently competed at the Six Sigma Slinger in Lower Lake on Sunday, April 16. It marked the last race of the team’s regular season before the NorCal Championship on Saturday and Sunday, May 6-7 at the same location. The Six Sigma Slinger featured a 4.5 miles course with an elevation gain of 575 feet. It was another big day for Piedmont High freshman Jasper Schuetz, who won the Div. 1 Freshman race with a two-lap time of 36:02.81, edging the nextbest rider, Alexander Tudor of Salinas, by 0.28 of a second. He has now won all four of his appearances this season and is likely going into the NorCal Championship as a favorite among freshman riders. In the varsity boys’ category, Andres Roberts finished 15th of 29 riders in the four-lap race. Aleksi Valkonen was 27th in 1:24:09. Close behind was Max Rivera in 17th, Matteo Scanu in 19th, and Schuyler Sawicki, 21st, Artun Duransoy was 43rd. In the Sophomore Boys’’ D1 event, Cary Ward finished 32nd. articles.text: Oversize Renaissance palaces, over some dozen, danced scenes played out on dual tiers. An oversize pit orchestra for the eloquent Prokofieff music, the most majestic ballet score of the 20th century, stamping this as the preeminent evening-length achievement of the post-Tchaikovsky era. All this and a massive cast set opulently in Shakespeare’s Verona. Can anything top this ballet for sheer performance power resonating with romanticism? And the feel of a lavish city state from half a millennium ago, with enough period costumes for half a dozen Italian masked balls. In the end, it comes down to the touching tragedy of Juliet who – sorry, Romeo –plays through three distinct phases of life. She ends up dead on her bier, fans crying in their beer, and she breaks every heart in the house. This is a “Romeo and Juliet” ballet to die for, a three-act spectacle and farewell message from the departed Helgi Tomasson and the late designer Jens-Jacob Worsaae in his final masterpiece, created at SF Ballet in 1994. The San Francisco Ballet put it all together for the April 21 opening, with a heroine from the lower ranks emerging, like some forgotten waif, to save the day in the role of Juliet. Tapped for the opener’s cast was a mere soloist, Jasmine Jimison of Palo Alto, with a colossal assignment given the competition of international artists on the SF Ballet roster. If Jasmine is not promoted to principal before the day is out, I’ll eat my Renaissance chapeau. On this very stage where Margot Fonteyn once ruled, this novice tackled the most baffling of all solo challenges in her long Indecision Scene, where acting must triumph over mere dancing. Like the proverbial cat on a hot tin roof, she vacillates, despairs, gravitates and zigzags with her quandary, close to madness: Face the parental orders to marry the bland suitor Paris, or risk possible death by taking the risky draught given her by the benevolent friar turned medicine-man Laurence. (Aficionados will recognize her telltale transition of letting down the long hair, usually verging on some mad scene, as Jimison had already demonstrated Photo by Lindsay Thomas Jasmine Jimison and Angelo Greco in Helgi Tomasson’s Romeo & Juliet in San Francisco Ballet’s current production. playing Giselle this winter.) Tearing around the stage like a trapped wild animal, she shows a rare ferocity, stamping her rare and too-long-overlooked talent. The young artist paired beautifully with the Romeo of Angelo Greco, a good-looking Italian-born matinee-idol type who on any other night might have stolen the show with his skyward leaps, whipping turns, and ferocious fencing to boot. He stands heroic among the five cadavers littering this drama, descending into an unforgettable love-death of a beloved doomed couple, deeply etched in memory after the last curtain. The stunning cast this night featured Luke Ingram as the murderous Tybalt, Esteban Hernández as the ill-fated cutup Mercutio, and the veteran Jim Sohm as the mortar-and-pestle Laurence. Casts change nightly. The oversize orchestra under Martin West was formidable, with the drama of unbridled French horns as well as an alto saxophone so popular in the East. And the lady next to us was ecstatic over the bright multicolor costumes for the huge cast. Last but not least, the most heated or elaborate of sword-fighting scenes were realistically done by Marco Pistone. BALLET NOTES Past performances of “R&J” on this very stage include the fabled mid-1960s pairing of Margot Fonteyn and Rudolf Nureyev, stars apprehended by the S.F. police after a show for attending a pot party, thereby upstaging their on-stage proficiency. In the 1970s Michael Smuin choreographed the world’s only Romeo and Juliet without the mandatory Balcony Scene, which contains one of the most romantic duos in all ballet, all because of production delays at the SFB. Later performances made up for it. A dispute over a possible happy ending, among other things, forced the original “R&J” ballet premiere to be shunting off to the capital of Moravia in 1938 before becoming a mainstay of Soviet ballet companies/ Sunday we learned of the shocking departure, after only one year, of SF Ballet exec director Danielle St. Germain, which 24 hours later the troupe was still unable to confirm. articles.text: Piedmont Center for the Arts will display a rare exhibit of the photos of the late Bay Area photographer James Mayer taken in Prague, Czechoslovakia the day the country was invaded by the Soviet Union in 1968. Mayer was a student traveling in Europe in 1968 and was in Prague on August 21, 1968. when Soviet tanks entered the streets of the country’s capital. He managed to document the action and get himself and his pictures out of the country. This is the first public exhibition of these stunning photos, strikingly familiar to the war in Ukraine today. His widow, Jane Flint, invites community members to a reception at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue, on Friday, April 28 from 6:00 to 8:00 p.m. The exhibit will also be open to the public on Saturday and Sunday, April 29-30 from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Background of Jim Mayer Jim Mayer graduated from Antioch College in Ohio, where his interest in photography (and motorcycles) grew and expanded to include proficiency in video and film. In his senior year abroad he happened to be in Prague, Czechoslovakia when the USSR invaded. He managed to get himself and the photographs of that event out to the Liberation News Service and the Los Angeles Free Press, which were the first to have footage of the invasion. After graduating, he moved to San Francisco and participated in Project One anchored by a organizations, including Optic Nerve, a photography collective co-founded by Mayer. Jim and Bill Bradbury introduced the group to the SONY Portapak, the first generation of portable video recorders that was instrumental in what came to be known as the Guerrilla Television Movement. Optic Nerve created several early documentaries that were among the first independently produced video documentaries to be broadcast on Public Television. In the late 60’s and early 70’s he studied Shaolin Kung-Fu and Lien-Ying style t’ai chi ch’uan at 5 a.m. in Portsmouth Square Park in San Francisco Chinatown. During the 70’s, he was employed at Xerox PARC in Palo Alto as a video specialist, documenting the many innovations developed at that time. In 1979, Jim, with Steve Christiansen and Lynn Adler, co-produced and directed Salmon On the Run, a documentary on competition between First People, sport fishers, and commercial fishers for the right to fish for Pacific salmon. The show was aired on the PBS science series NOVA. In 1980, Jim, with Optic Nerve A Soviet tank is surrounded by Czech citizens after Prague was invaded on August 21, 1968. Bay Area photographer Jim Mayer at Sutro Heights in San Francisco in 1988 members John Rogers and Lynn Adler, formed Ideas In Motion, continuing the ideals of Optic Nerve within a sustainable financial structure. For 40 years, Jim and his partners created documentaries, sponsored video, and commissioned work, addressing social issues and celebrating the creative spirit. In recent years he also spearheaded a series of videos on the intricacies of complicated watchmaking in Switzerland. He was fully in his element in a breakneck production schedule, doing the work he loved, whether in the ateliers of Le Brassus, or under the streets of Queens. Since its founding, Ideas In Motion provided pro bono video services for Bay Area arts organizations, including the Pickle Family Circus and the San Francisco Mime Troupe. Amazingly, he still found time to restore a MK II 3.8 Jaguar, study Russian Constructivist art and experimental cinema, read extensively on WW2 espionage, develop a good knowledge of French wine and Scotch whiskey, cook, garden, and in later life even took up the clarinet, playing with the Musicians’ Action Group of Berkeley and marching with them in the May Day Parade in Paris in 2016 with a host of other international political action bands. articles.text: Angela Davis: Seize the Time, an exhibition celebrating the political activist, is on display at the Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) now through June 11. Born In Birmingham, Alabama in 1944, Davis is best known as an African American activist and educator who championed civil rights and other social issues, from racial equity to women’s rights and lesbian, gay and transgender rights. She has written Women and Race & Class, Are Prisons Obsolete?, Abolition Democracy, and The Meaning of Freedom. Davis was a professor at the UC Santa Cruz, where she taught courses on the history of consciousness. She retired in 2008. Political activist Angela Davis The exhibition was organized by OMCA in partnership with the Zimmerli Art Museum at Rutgers University, and features photographs and personal entries from the Angela Davis Archive in Oakland. articles.text: Aurora Theatre is now showing Cyrano onstage through May 7. Based upon the story of Cyrano de Bergerac, written by Edmond Rostand in 1897, the current adaptation is directed by Aurora Theatre Artistic Director Josh Costello. It is a classic tale of Cyrano, who is fearless in battle and swordplay but shy in confronting Roxanne, the woman he loves. Ashamed of his appearance (an oversize nose), he enlists the help of Christian, who has a pretty face but lacks the gift of gab. Costello turns the odd love triangle into an intimate play of life and love. The cast includes William Thomas Hodgson as Cyrano, Leontyne Mbele-Mbong as Roxanne, and Ron Campbell, Adrian Roberts and Steven Flores. Post-show discussions will be held on April 26 and May 4, moderated by Associate Artistic Director Dawn Monique Williams. Visit https://www.auroratheatre.org for showtimes and to purchase tickets. articles.text: Everyone knows Einstein’s famous theory; E= MC squared. Likewise, most people knows that Einstein loved music and the violin. Continuing this line of reasoning, let’s add two equations to baffle Einstein. We can have the famous professor act as the judge, but you need to be the jury. A unanimous decision is not required. • Formula number one: Technique+ personality = artistry • Formula number two: Technique+torque = success My wife’s birthday celebration gave us the perfect excuse to take in a concert of the Monterey Symphony over the weekend. I am a fan of the NPR program “From the Top”. One of the co-hosts is the young Violinist Tessa Lark. Her repartee with host Peter Dugan is always lively and adds immeasurably to the program itself. When I found out that Tessa Lark was playing a concert with the Monterey Symphony our weekend was predetermined. We arrived at the Sunset Theater in time to hear some of the rehearsal. The violinist and the orchestra were rehearsing Sibelius’ famous Violin Concerto. This was indeed fortunate because it gave me the opportunity to hear both the rehearsal and the concert on the same day. It is fun to eavesdrop on the inner workings. The concert was devoted entirely to the music of Sibelius. It began with Lark playing the violin concerto. She is a statuesque woman with a commanding presence. Likewise, most people knows that Einstein loved music and the violin. Continuing this line of reasoning, let’s add two equations to baffle Einstein. We can have the famous professor act as the judge, but you need to be the jury. A unanimous decision is not required. • Formula number one: Technique+ personality = artistry • Formula number two: Technique+torque = success My wife’s birthday celebration gave us the perfect excuse to take in a concert of the Monterey Symphony over the weekend. I am a fan of the NPR program “From the Top”. One of the co-hosts is the young Violinist Tessa Lark. Her repartee with host Peter Dugan is always lively and adds immeasurably to the program itself. When I found out that Tessa Lark was playing a concert with the Monterey Symphony our weekend was predetermined. We arrived at the Sunset Theater in time to hear some of the rehearsal. The violinist and the orchestra were rehearsing Sibelius’ famous Violin Concerto. This was indeed fortunate because it gave me the opportunity to hear both the rehearsal and the concert on the same day. It is fun to eavesdrop on the inner workings. The concert was devoted entirely to the music of Sibelius. It began with Lark playing the violin concerto. She is a statuesque woman with a commanding presence. Her violinistic arsenal is abetted by a solid technique and a big tone. Like many performers of her generation, her playing is absolutely perfect technically speaking, and a perfect example of my formula number two. I continue to be amazed by the abilities of today’s young performers. Perfection is their way of life. They simply don’t make mistakes. What I miss in today’s performers is a readily identifiable personality. Lark’s performance at Monterey wowed the audience. We were rewarded with the dividend of some high-level country fiddlin’. The new conductor, Jayce Ogren, inspires the orchestra with his energetic presence. Soloist, conductor, and orchestra were in perfect alignment in the Sibelius violin concerto. articles.text: An assortment of Bay Area comedians and diverse comedy formats will be converging on Saturday, May 6 at Piedmont Center for the Arts for the inaugural production of “Something Humorous,” a variety show organized and hosted by Piedmont-based comedian Barry Fischer. Headlining the night will be “The Right Now,” an acclaimed three-woman group of free-form improv blending highly physical short vignettes with longer character-driven scenes. Group members Claire Slattery, Fontana Butterfield, and Mariah Howard play across gender, genre, and form, and are known for their fast-paced wit and seamless transitions. The trio has delighted crowds across a range of prestigious stages, including the San Francisco Improv Festival, SF Sketchfest, Out of Bounds Comedy Festival in Austin, and Blast Theater Festival in Berkeley. Piedmont High alumna and actress Claire Neumann will offer a high-energy dose of comedic musical theater. While at PHS in the early 2000s, Claire twice won the Bird Calling Contest. After graduating from Northwestern University, she became a professional actress and starred in a number of major productions. She’s taken on notable roles in the National Tour of Charlie and The Chocolate Factory, Baghdaddy (a NYTimes’ Critic’s pick and musical about the Iraq War), and the acclaimed Off-Broadway musical Triassic Parq (in which Claire played a dinosaur exploring their gender identity). She was also nominated for Best Actress for her portrayal of Annie Oakley in Annie Get Your Gun and Nellie in Floyd Collins at the Weathervane Theatre. Three other local stand-up comedians and Bay Area music veteran David Steinberg will round out the show. Performance time is 7:30 p.m. on Saturday, May 6, preceded by an outdoor reception on the lawn at 7 p.m. A limited number of tickets remain and are available at www.somethinghumorous.com.

pages.text: 20 Wednesday, Aprl 26, 2023 MOVIES FOR ADULTS Plenty to think about in Clouds of Sils Maria By Chris Honore’ The title, Clouds of Sils Maria, is a metaphor. Sils Maria is a mountain range surrounding the Engadine Valley in the Swiss Alps, known for its ethereal cloud formations that slide out of the mountains like a long snake and move inextricably closer to a glacial lake and village. It portends the coming of bad weather. The film opens with Maria Enders (Juliette Binoche), renowned actress, and her assistant, Valentine (Kristen Stewart), on a train heading toward Zurich for a celebratory dinner to be held in honor of her mentor, famous playwright and filmmaker, Wilhelm Melchior. While en route, Maria learns that Melchior has died of a heart attack and suddenly the dinner and anticipated award becomes a eulogy. She also meets in Zurich a highly regarded young director who wants her to agree to do a play, Majola Snake, written and produced by Mechior some 20 tears earlier, and one in which Maria starred as a young unknown actor. The role launched her career. Instead of playing the youthful ingénue (her original role), she will play the older woman, a role about which she feels great uncertainty. An American starlet, Jo-Ann Ellis, (Chloe Grace Juliet Binoche and Kristen Stewart in Clouds of Sils Maria Moretz), who relishes scandal, has been cast as the seductive, manipulating young woman. Maria, for all of her fame, is a woman in midlife crisis, going through a divorce. She is reluctant to fully acknowledge that her youth, and all its allure, is now part of her past. She is, after countless films, someone else. And so she and Valentine retreat to Melchior’s Swiss chalet near Sils Maria where they will rehearse the lines to the play while discussing the characters, especially the older woman that Maria will try to inhabit. Clouds is a film carried by dialogue – lots of dialogue. Val and Maria discuss, spar, argue, drink too much and talk some more. Their relationship bluntly mirrors the play and often it is difficult to know if the encounters they are having are part of the play or simply a harsh and confrontational conversation. While the film has moments that are interesting, and Binoche is clearly a an enormously gifted performer, the narrative seems stilted and even uninteresting. It can feel inaccessible and obscure. As Maria and Val slip from scene to scene, dinner, breakfast, rehearsal, lunch, it can all seem flat, making it difficult to care about the characters. Yes, the point made over and over is that art and life can merge as boundaries fall away. What is fact and what is fiction? But for “Clouds” to touch the audience it must reach for more, for an intimacy, for clarity, for depth as well as breadth, which it fails to do. Binoche is courageous and the camera often lingers on her mature, stunning beauty. Stewart, though reaping much praise for her portrayal as Maria’s bright factotum, seems to have only one gear and that is Stewart doing Stewart. She fidgets, smokes, and debates pop culture and pop movies with Maria and still sounds like a quasi-rebellious teenager whose life experiences remain truncated. But then so much of this movie feels the same way: still unformed, even purposely ambiguous. Clouds of Sils Maria . Directed by Oliver Assayas. Starring Juliet Binoche, Kristen Stewart and Chloe Grace Moretz. 2 hrs., 3 min. Rated R. Released 2015. Streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Apple tv. articles.text: The character Astro Boy was created in 1951 by the celebrated animator of Japanese manga (comic books), Osamu Tezuka. In the 1960s, Astro, originally known as Tetsuwan Atomu (Mighty Atom), appeared in a popular television show, viewed in more than 40 countries, and now Astro makes his debut in a feature film. For children today, Astro Boy will be new and fresh. They will be captivated by the story and the nonstop action. This first installment explains how a young boy, Toby (Freddy Highmore), is killed in an experiment conducted by his scientist father, Dr. Tenma (Nicolas Cage). Wracked with grief and guilt, Tenma creates an exact replica of his son, a small android, giving him all of Toby’s memories and a heart of “blue power” which makes the boy (soon to be called Astro) superhuman. He can fly, has machine guns in his butt, x-ray vision, amazing strength, and rockets in his shoes and hands. Astro, at first unaware he’s a robot, sets out to find his place in the world, meaning, Metro City, an urban island hovering above earth which has been turned into a dumpsite for outdated robots and broken machinery. After being rejected by his father, who cannot accept that he’s a robot, Astro goes to earth and meets a group of kids, orphans from Metro City, all his own age. These discarded kids have no families. They are, however, human and Astro is reluctant to disclose that he is not. And so the story goes. The kids long for Astro’s powers and he longs for their humanity. He also grieves for the loss of his father. There’s an evil Mayor of Metro City (Donald Sutherland) who covets Astro’s “blue power,” a duplicitous hustler named Hamegg (Nathan Lane) who wants only to use Astro, and, finally, a long journey back into the arms of his dad. While the story brings to mind Transformers and Pinocchio (likely not known to young filmgoers), kids will find Astro appealing and can look forward to a sequel, The Return of Astro Boy. As t ro Boy. articles.text: The arrival of extra-terrestrials on earth has been a staple of science fiction filmmaking since celluloid clicked through a theater camera, casting grainy images on a large white screen. More often than not, the intentions of the visitors are malevolent and things generally do not end well for mankind or the E.T.s. It’s a well-established and popular genre. But know – and this is really important – that Arrival is far more thoughtful and cerebral than what the title implies. This is not your standard issue War of the Worlds sci-fi film. Instead, it’s a remarkable puzzle that bends time and situations and relationships in a series of carefully crafted reveals. Know also that writing about this film is dicey. To allow the filmgoer to screen this film with no preconceptions while reviewing it is challenging at best. What can be disclosed – and I believe this appeared not only on the movie’s posters but also in the trailer – is that 12 enormous ships appear around the world, each hovering mere feet off the ground. One is in Montana. The existential questions posed by this dark shape’s ominous presence are: Why is it here? What are its intentions? How do we communicate with those inside? Okay, here’s a bit more. The military (uncertain as to whether the visitors pose a threat or come in peace) reaches out to professor Louise Banks (Amy Adams), a renowned linguist, who is joined by theoretical physicist, Ian Donnelly (Jeremy Renner). They are tasked with decoding their language (strange circles and unusual sounds) and establishing contact. What Arrival is about is language. Can Banks and Donnelly construct a bridge of common understanding that will allow them (and those waiting) to know why the visitors are here? The stakes are high as paranoia begins to creep into the analysis by multiple countries. Meanwhile, in f lashing images, shown via news stations, the world’s population is either deeply fearful, in the grips of a rising panic, or on the verge of mass riots. But this is not a story about finding out we are not alone in the universe. It is instead about overcoming a seemingly impenetrable code. The film is also intercut with images of Banks with her daughter, at first an infant and then growing into a young woman. These are touching scenes that set the stage for an overwhelming grief. How her relationship to her daughter is relevant to the superordinate narrative remains opaque throughout until the final reveal which will likely cause much discussion. The sense of disorientation and ambiguity lasts well beyond the final credits. There is also the possibility that the film is an allegory suggesting that language is fundamental to our humanness. When we stop believing in the magic of language, we can feel a sense of isolation and loneliness. Language shapes us, defines us, and it is something we struggle with each waking moment as we strive to understand and be genuinely heard. That is the communication dilemma posed by this amazing film, based on the sci-fi short story by Ted Chiang and now directed by the gifted French-Canadian Denis Villeneuve (Sicario). Science Fiction has recently experienced a surprising renaissance with films such as Gravity, Interstellar, Ex-Machina and The Martian. Add Arrival to that list – less linear and even confounding, it is worth every moment. Arrival. Directed by Dennis Villeneuv. Starring Amy Adams, Jeremy Renner, Forest Whitaker. 1 hr., 56 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2016, Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.

Astro Boy a fresh series from Japanese manga By Chris Honore’ The character Astro Boy was created in 1951 by the celebrated animator of Japanese manga (comic books), Osamu Tezuka. In the 1960s, Astro, originally known as Tetsuwan Atomu (Mighty Atom), appeared in a popular television show, viewed in more than 40 countries, and now Astro makes his debut in a feature film. For children today, Astro Boy will be new and fresh. They will be captivated by the story and the nonstop action. This first installment explains how a young boy, Toby (Freddy Highmore), is killed in an experiment conducted by his scientist father, Dr. Tenma (Nicolas Cage). Wracked with grief and guilt, Tenma creates an exact replica of his son, a small android, giving him all of Toby’s memories and a heart of “blue power” which makes the boy (soon to be called Astro) superhuman. He can fly, has machine guns in his butt, x-ray vision, amazing strength, and rockets in his shoes and hands. Astro, at first unaware he’s a robot, sets out to find his place in the world, meaning, Metro City, an urban island hovering above earth which has been turned into a dumpsite for outdated robots and broken machinery. After being rejected by his father, who cannot accept that he’s a robot, Astro goes to earth and meets a group of kids, orphans from Metro City, all his own age. These discarded kids have no families. They are, however, human and Astro is reluctant to disclose that he is not. And so the story goes. The kids long for Astro’s powers and he longs for their humanity. He also grieves for the loss of his father. There’s an evil Mayor of Metro City (Donald Sutherland) who covets Astro’s “blue power,” a duplicitous hustler named Hamegg (Nathan Lane) who wants only to use Astro, and, finally, a long journey back into the arms of his dad. While the story brings to mind Transformers and Pinocchio (likely not known to young filmgoers), kids will find Astro appealing and can look forward to a sequel, The Return of Astro Boy. As t ro Boy. articles.text: Many of the clients we work with have never engaged an architect and therefore come into the process of remodeling or building a new home knowing very little of the steps of developing a design and bringing it into construction. We have become accustomed to educating our clients about this process and guiding them through it step-by-step until the project is done. Whether the project is small and simple to very complex, many of the steps are the same. For the purposes of this article, we will concentrate on remodel projects rather than new home projects. At the start of a remodel project, we try to understand and help clarify the client’s Program for the project. The Program in the simplest terms is what you are trying to accomplish: more space, bigger spaces for some areas of the house, new kitchen, bathroom remodel, extra bedrooms, developing a basement, etc. The Program may also relate information about how spaces connect to one another, as well as incorporate a description of the desired look and feel. The first step is to develop As-Built Drawings of the existing house or portion of the house. If it is a major remodel, we may do a site analysis to determine how to situate the spaces of the house to maximize access to natural light and views. The next step is to develop a Preliminary Design. Depending on the project, we will develop sketches of possible solutions to the layout and flow issues we are trying to solve. We like to develop multiple ideas to offer alternative approaches. Once an approach to the layout is selected, we do a Design Development process. Here we like to do some 3D modeling to flesh out the design character of the spaces or exterior work. More detailed drawings are developed with notations. These drawings are used to informally discuss with agency staff of the local Building and Planning Departments. Depending on the project, one may need to go through a formal Design Review process. A ballpark pricing exercise with a contractor is also often developed at this time. After any necessary Planning Department approvals are achieved and the preliminary ballpark pricing is in alignment with the client’s budget, we develop the more detailed Permit Drawings and subsequent Construction Drawings. Then we can do the final pricing or bidding with contractors. The advantages of negotiation with a single pre-qualified contractor early in the process vs. having multiple contractors bid only after construction drawings have been completed is the subject of another article. Walkers By Dick Carter A great turnout of 53 walkers and four K-9 best friends showed up on April 19 for the fifth anniversary of the Walking on Wednesday group. A lot has happened since the group’s first walk on April 18, 2018 with 17 people. Covid shut most things in 2020, but the group came back in 2021 and has grown even stronger. It currently has 184 members. Thanks were given to architect Jim Kellogg who the week before took the group on an architectural tour of homes designed by noted early 20th Century architects. There was another thank you, too. On the group’s first walk Gail Lombardi, president of the Piedmont Historical Society, provided a tour of buildings in the center of Piedmont. Gail wasn’t able to be with the walkers last Wednesday, but her research in Piedmont Post articles has provided information for many walks. Five of Gail’s articles about Piedmont Park provided historical content for the day’s tour. It started with recalling that Walter Blair, the first European settler in the area, bought 600 acres in what is now Piedmont in 1852 for $750, and that Isaac Holmes discovered mineral springs in the Park’s Bushy Dell Creek about this time. The entrepreneurial Blair built horse trolley lines from Oakland to the Piedmont Springs Hotel that he and investors built in 1872 on an additional 350 acres. They selected the name “Piedmont,” meaning “foot of the hills.” Blair died in 1888 at the young age of 57, which spared him seeing his hotel burn to the ground four years later. Land developer Frank C. Havens entered the scene about this time and decided the mineral springs would be a great attraction for potential land buyers, and he began developing Piedmont Park. The walkers were told that Piedmont Park across from Wells Fargo Bank was where Havens built a firstclass dining room in 1898. He also cleared the vegetation in the ravine below and created a Victorian strolling park with a Japanese Tea House, built as replica of a 15th Century tea house in Kyoto. The current Japanese tea house in Piedmont Park came from a residence on Hillside Avenue when Piedmont Middle School was being built in 1976. The group learned that the location of the current tennis courts in Piedmont Park behind the Community Hall was the location where Havens built his Piedmont Art Gallery with a collection of 375 paintings. It was one of the finest collections in the country. Continuing on the park’s lower trail along Bushy Dell Creek, they passed Havens’ “Cascades” and a grotto where Mark Twain once sampled the mineral springs in the 1860s. They emerged at Witter Field, a natural bowl where Havens created a large circular hedge maze attraction in 1904. Havens got into financial difficulties, and by 1916 he was planning on developing the park for residential sites. However, the land went into foreclosure and the park was to be sold. The school board wanted to buy 13 acres for a new high school and Piedmont philanthropist Wallace Alexander purchased 14 acres for a park, for which the City later reimbursed him. With their park tour complete it was time to return to the Tea House for lunch. articles.text: The Rev. Tom Trutner was called home peacefully on February 1, 2023 surrounded by family and dear friends. He was 87. Tom shall be remembered for many gifts, but none more memorable than happy hugs and his “cheerful easy smile.” He greeted both friend and stranger alike with a sense of genuine warmth and acceptance, and though he was known to his parishioners as “Father Tom,” he would have been just as pleased with “Brother” - Saint Francis was his patron saint, and The Blessing of The Animals was one of his favorite Holy blessings. Born Thomas Kirk Trutner on May 25, 1935, he was the son of Herman and Evelyn Trutner and the younger brother of Tony (Anton) and Fritzi (Frederika). Their grandfather, Herman Cameron Trutner II, was a noted Bay Area conductor and music teacher. His father played the French horn for the San Francisco Symphony and the San Francisco Opera Company. Having grown up with two professional musicians in the family influenced Tom’s preferred listening choice and that was classical – always classical. After graduating from Piedmont High School in 1953, where played quarterback for the football team with his best friend Monte Upshaw, and many others who also became lifelong friends, he completed his undergraduate studies at UC Berkeley and graduated in 1958. He joined the Beta Theta Pi fraternity and began to play the “gentleman’s sport” of rugby. After Cal his decision to attend Princeton Seminary was life-changing. One of his favorite professors was the Scottish minister Ernest Gordon, the author of Miracle on the Kwai. Gordon’s experience as a World War II prisoner in a Japanese camp was transformative for Tom, who learned how men, who left to die, were aided by fellow prisoners encouraging them to live. They “put their feet to their faith” and saved even the sickest. That message of faith set Tom on a life-long path. While at Princeton, he played rugby for three more years and became a “Rugger” for life. Years later, Tom became one of the co-founders of the Old Blues Rugby Club, a team that competed Rev. Tom Trutner in prayer at St. Paul’s Episcopal Church in Oakland. nationally and internationally, winning the first United States National Club Championship in 1979. After seminary, Tom traveled to Hamburg, Germany with his young family and worked as an associate pastor in a local church. The experience of living abroad led to a lifetime of Tom taking students, parishioners, and friends touring throughout Europe. His philosophy regarding travel was: Visit the cities for their cultural richness found in museums, churches, art galleries, and architecture. Then drive to the towns and villages, sampling their food and local customs. And finally, check out the festivals, for “therein lies the spirit of the people.” Tom loved the family he came from and cherished the family he created with his first wife, Shirlee Jones Sampsel, and their son, Kirk, who became his father’s closest companion and golf partner. Years later, with his subsequent marriage to Jackie Milton O’Connor, he became a stepfather to four boys, Max, Bill and Jim Milton, and Matt O’Connor. Sadly, after 21 years of a wonderful marriage, his beloved Jackie succumbed to ALS, surrounded by all of her children and grandchildren. I n 2001, Tom became acquainted with Roxanna Smith Wing while tossing a football at Bishop’s Ranch Episcopal Retreat in Healdsburg. They were married the following year at the Ranch with Tom becoming once again a stepfather, this time to Roxanna’s daughter, Bria, and her two half-brothers, Rich and Jon Wing. Tom chose to balance his career between the secular community and the church. Of his 55 years in the ministry, 20 were served in the Presbyterian Church and 35 as an Episcopal priest. His career spanned Piedmont Community Church: Youth Director and Camp Director at Lodestar, 1967-70; University of California Berkeley Associate Dean of Students, Student Orientation program (CalSO), Fundraising Chair, School of Optometry, 1970-1987; St. Paul’s Episcopal Church, Oakland, 1978-1987; Associate Priest, Stephens Episcopal Church, Orinda, 1987- 2020. He also shared a Marriage, Family, and Child counseling practice with his good friend Sharon Gillan, and a travel business with Guyla Cashel. Father Tom became the person so many families turned to in times of both sorrow and joy. When he retired he was marrying the children of the couples he previously married over a span of 61 years. Tom recently commented, “I am 87 years old, and I’ve had a good life”. Indeed, he did - he had an extraordinary one. Those meeting Tom for the first time were impressed by his kindness and curiosity, and those who knew him best were touched by his sincere caring and keen interest in their lives. It is we who are left behind who feel that deep sense of loss, yet we are so grateful for the joy he so generously shared with us, and the delightful memories made together. Tom is survived by his wife Roxanne, son Kirk, seven stepchildren, 13 grandchildren, and 10 great-grandchildren. “All shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well.” A memorial service for Tom Trutner will be held at the Lafayette-Orinda Presbyterian Church on Saturday, April 29 at 11:00 a.m., with a reception to follow.

articles.text: Helen Steers, a longtime Piedmont resident, passed away peacefully on Monday, April 10, 2023. Born in 1943 in Northern Wales to Evan and Margaret, she moved to the U.S. in 1971 after meeting and marrying Jim Steers of Piedmont. She was hired by Tulloch Construction in 1971 and continued working there for nearly 50 years. She was an active member of Piedmont Community Church for over 45 years, sand served as a Deacon and in many other capacities. She loved to knit with the church Needles and Hooks Club. Her retirement years were spent travelling, spending time with her grandchildren, walking around town, gardening, engaging in public service, and indulging in British crime dramas. While she was very proud of obtaining her U.S. Citizenship, she also loved humor, quiet strength, and selfless generosity of her time. She is deeply missed by her many family members and friends. Helen is survived by her daughter Carys and son-in-law Ben of Alameda, and by son Andrew and daughter-in-law Amanda Steers in South Carolina. She is additionally survived by grandchildren Jamie and Sawyer, Anderson and Alice, her sister Phyllis, brother David, and many cousins, nephews, nieces, grandnephews and grandnieces in both Wales and California. A memorial gathering of family and friends, to honor Helen will be held on May 6, 2023, at Piedmont Community Church at 2 p.m. The family suggests that in lieu of flowers, consider making donations in her name to a local food bank, the SPCA, or a charity of your choice. articles.text: REAL ESTATE AND PIEDMONT TAXES Along with spring’s beautiful flowers comes tax season. Let’s delve into a conversation about two types of taxes that are associated with our homes: property taxes and city transfer taxes. We’ll do our best not to create tax-related anxiety or lull you to sleep with our research! Piedmont’s 2022-2023 Fiscal Year Budget estimates its property tax funds budget at nearly $17M and city transfer tax funds at an estimated $3.2M. PROPERTY TAXES According to the California Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO), “a typical California property tax bill consists of many taxes and charges including the “1 percent rate” (part of the “Ad Valorem Tax” on each bill that goes to the County), voter-approved debt rates, parcel taxes, Mello-Roos taxes, and assessments.” Our homebuyer clients often ask us “How much should I expect to pay in property taxes each year?” The answer is “it depends.” For new homeowners, the majority of their property tax bill comes from taxes and charges that are calculated based on their assessed value. However, charges can also be based on the square footage of your home or parcel. Consequently, there is no fixed property tax rate. Taxes vary by house, city, neighborhood, and parcel. Our new homeowners can usually expect to pay around 1.4 - 1.6 % of their home’s assessed value in the first year. RECENT HISTORY OF PIEDMONT TRANSFER TAXES 2004-2021 Source: City of Piedmont Budget for Fiscal Year 2022-2023 CITY TRANSFER TAXES In Piedmont, every time a home is sold there is a city transfer tax paid by the buyers and sellers in the transaction (typically split 50%/50%). The city transfer tax is $13 per 1,000 of the property’s purchase price, or $13,000 per $1 million in home sales. Is the City on track to meet its FY 2022-2023 transfer tax estimate of $3.2M? It is! We looked at Piedmont home sales from July 1, 2022 to the most recent sales recorded at the County of Alameda and found that the City of Piedmont has already received nearly $3.5M in city transfer taxes with more than two months left before the end of the fiscal year. JUST FOR FUN: SALES TAX BONUS DATA When you buy items for your home, you pay sales tax too. Cities in Alameda County have the highest sales taxes in the state. Los Angeles County comes in a close second. Most CA counties sales tax rates range between 7 - 9%.
